questions.q: Breech is the m/c malpresentation with longitudinal lie and breech/podalic presentation. Match incidence – 28 wks : 34 wks : term.
opts: About 25% at 28 weeks, 5% at 34 weeks and 3-4% at term, as most turn spontaneously
About 3-4% at 28 weeks, 5% at 34 weeks and 25% at term, as more turn with time
About 50% at 28 weeks, 25% at 34 weeks and 10% at term in most series
About 10% at 28 weeks, 3% at 34 weeks and 1% at term after routine version
questions.exp: Breech is common early and uncommon at term because most babies turn by themselves as gestation advances. (Book p550)

questions.q: M/c cause of breech overall and of recurrent breech:
opts: Prematurity, since spontaneous rotation has not yet occurred; uterine malformation
Uterine malformation; prematurity, since spontaneous rotation has not yet occurred
Placenta previa preventing engagement; uterine fibroids distorting the cavity
Oligohydramnios limiting movement; multiple pregnancy crowding the cavity
questions.exp: The commonest cause of breech overall is prematurity (spontaneous rotation has not yet occurred) and of recurrent breech is uterine malformation. (Book p550)

questions.q: Match the posture – Flexed/complete breech : Frank breech : Knee presentation : Footling breech.
opts: Hips and knees flexed : hips flexed, knees extended : hips extended, knees flexed : hips and knees extended
Hips flexed, knees extended : hips and knees flexed : hips and knees extended : hips extended, knees flexed
Hips and knees extended : hips and knees flexed : hips flexed, knees extended : hips extended, knees flexed
Hips extended, knees flexed : hips flexed, knees extended : hips and knees flexed : hips and knees extended
questions.exp: Complete: hips + knees flexed; frank: hips flexed/knees extended; knee: hips extended/knees flexed; footling: both extended. (Book p550)

questions.q: Structures felt on vaginal examination — complete breech : frank breech : knee : footling.
opts: Complete: heel, anus and ischial tuberosities — frank: anus and tuberosities — knee: knees — footling: feet
Complete: feet only — frank: knees — knee: heel and anus — footling: anus and tuberosities
Complete: anus only — frank: feet — knee: heel — footling: knees
Complete: sacrum and anus — frank: feet — knee: anus — footling: knees
questions.exp: The more the legs are extended, the less is felt: complete breech gives heel, anus and tuberosities, footling breech gives only the feet. (Book p550)

questions.q: Occurrence – complete breech : frank breech.
opts: Least common breech overall, commonest in multigravida : commonest overall and in primigravida
Commonest breech overall : the least common breech variety
Commonest in primigravida : commonest in multigravida
Both occur with equal frequency in all parities
questions.exp: Complete breech is the least common breech overall and the commonest in multigravida; frank breech is the commonest overall and in primigravida. (Book p550)

questions.q: Risk of cord prolapse across breech types:
opts: Frank breech lowest, complete breech low, knee presentation higher and footling highest
Frank breech highest, complete breech next, knee lower and footling presentation lowest
The risk of cord prolapse is identical for all four types of breech presentation
Complete breech highest, footling next, knee lower and frank breech lowest
questions.exp: Cord prolapse risk rises as the presenting part fits the cervix less well: frank breech is snug, footling breech is not. (Book p550)

questions.q: Match the type of breech with its posture — 1) Frank breech 2) Complete breech 3) Footling breech … A) Hips and knees both flexed, so the feet lie beside the buttocks B) Hips flexed with both knees extended, so the feet lie up beside the head C) One or both legs extended below the buttocks, carrying the highest risk of cord prolapse
questions.exp: Frank breech has extended legs, complete breech is the fully flexed 'cannonball' posture, and footling breech risks cord prolapse. (Book p550)

questions.q: Overall ranking of cord prolapse risk and the m/c position in breech:
opts: Transverse lie > footling breech > knee presentation; dorso-anterior
Footling > transverse > frank; dorso-posterior
Knee > footling > transverse; sacro-posterior
Frank > complete > footling; LSA
questions.exp: Cord prolapse: transverse lie > footling > knee; m/c breech position dorso-anterior. (Book p551)

questions.sec: Management of breech: USG, ECV & mode of delivery
questions.q: USG in breech is used to confirm diagnosis, assess type (rule out ECV C/I) and to rule out:
opts: Gross congenital anomalies, hyperextension of the fetal neck and an estimated fetal weight at or above 4 kg
Placenta previa, oligohydramnios and a single loop of cord around the fetal neck
Cord presentation, vasa previa and a velamentous insertion of the umbilical cord
Fetal hydrocephalus, duodenal atresia and bilateral renal agenesis
questions.exp: Ultrasound looks for the three findings that contraindicate external cephalic version: anomalies, a stargazer neck and a heavy fetus. (Book p551)

questions.sec: Management of breech: USG, ECV & mode of delivery
questions.q: ECV flowchart for breech at term with no C/I (done in OPD at >37 weeks) – successful : unsuccessful : fetal distress.
opts: Successful: send her home to await labour — unsuccessful: a second attempt, else elective caesarean — fetal distress: stop and deliver
Successful: induce labour immediately — unsuccessful: caesarean section — fetal distress: continue the attempt
Successful: caesarean at 39 weeks — unsuccessful: retry later the same day — fetal distress: give oxytocin
Successful: send her home — unsuccessful: caesarean at 37 weeks — fetal distress: retry the version
questions.exp: After a successful version the woman goes home to labour; a failed attempt is retried, and any fetal distress ends the procedure. (Book p551)

questions.sec: Management of breech: USG, ECV & mode of delivery
questions.q: Modes of delivery in breech and preference:
opts: Caesarean section >> assisted breech delivery
Assisted breech >> C-section
Breech extraction >> C-section
Equal preference
questions.exp: C-section is strongly preferred over assisted breech delivery. (Book p551)

questions.sec: Management of breech: USG, ECV & mode of delivery
questions.q: Which of the following statements about the management of breech presentation is TRUE?
opts: External cephalic version from 36-37 weeks with tocolysis reduces the chance of caesarean section in suitable women
External cephalic version should be attempted during labour after the membranes have ruptured
Every breech at term must be delivered by caesarean section without offering version
Planned vaginal breech delivery is recommended for all women who request it, whatever the fetal size or position
questions.exp: External cephalic version before labour improves the chance of cephalic birth; vaginal breech is limited to strict criteria and skilled attendance. (Book p551)

questions.sec: Management of breech: USG, ECV & mode of delivery
questions.q: Absolute indications for C-section in breech include all EXCEPT:
opts: Primigravida with breech (this is a RELATIVE indication)
Footling/knee/stargazer breech (ECV C/I) and preterm breech/weight <1.5 kg
Post-term or baby >4 kg, 1st twin breech, previous C-section
PIH/placenta previa, breech score ≤3, protracted active phase (treated as CPD)
questions.exp: Primigravida with breech is a relative indication; the others are absolute. (Book p552)

questions.sec: Management of breech: USG, ECV & mode of delivery
questions.q: Protracted active phase (delay in 1st/2nd stage) in a breech is considered as ______ and managed by ______.
opts: CPD; immediate C-section
Normal; oxytocin
Malposition; wait
Uterine inertia; ARM
questions.exp: Delay in breech labour = CPD → immediate C-section. (Book p552)

questions.sec: Assisted breech delivery: features, complication, C/I & prerequisites
questions.q: Assisted breech delivery – denominator : engaging diameter : m/c position.
opts: Sacrum : bitrochanteric (10 cm) : left sacro-anterior (LSA)
Sacrum : bisacromial (12 cm) : RSA
Ischium : bitrochanteric : DSA
Coccyx : biparietal : LSP
questions.exp: Denominator sacrum; bitrochanteric 10 cm; LSA m/c. (Book p552)

questions.sec: Assisted breech delivery: features, complication, C/I & prerequisites
questions.q: Main complication of vaginal breech delivery:
opts: The after-coming head becomes trapped, causing fetal hypoxia and intracranial haemorrhage
Shoulder dystocia with brachial plexus injury from traction on the extended arms
Uterine inversion from traction on the cord during delivery of the placenta
Cord avulsion with fetal exsanguination before the trunk has been delivered
questions.exp: The deadly complication of breech delivery is entrapment of the after-coming head, which is why the head must never be rushed. (Book p552)

questions.sec: Assisted breech delivery: features, complication, C/I & prerequisites
questions.q: Contraindications in assisted breech (and all malpresentations):
opts: Induction and augmentation of labour, since rupturing the membranes invites cord prolapse
Epidural analgesia, which abolishes the urge to push and prevents descent
Continuous cardiotocography, which alarms and forces unnecessary intervention
An episiotomy, which risks extending into the anal sphincter during a breech birth
questions.exp: An intact sac protects against cord prolapse in malpresentation, so induction and augmentation are avoided; analgesia and monitoring are not contraindications. (Book p552)

questions.sec: Assisted breech delivery: features, complication, C/I & prerequisites
questions.q: Prerequisites for assisted breech delivery:
opts: Emergency C-section facility, senior supervision, baby under 4 kg, IV fluids, CTG
Emergency C-section facility, senior supervision, baby up to 4.5 kg, oral fluids
Emergency C-section facility, registrar alone, baby under 4 kg, intermittent CTG
Emergency C-section facility, senior supervision, baby under 4 kg, no CTG needed
questions.exp: Assisted breech delivery requires a centre with emergency C-section facilities, senior supervision, an estimated fetal weight under 4 kg, nil by mouth with IV fluids, and continuous CTG monitoring. (Book p552)

questions.q: All of the following are prerequisites for assisted breech delivery EXCEPT:
opts: Intact membranes with the forewaters bulging
Full cervical dilatation with an empty bladder and rectum
A flexed head confirmed by ultrasound before the attempt
Continuous fetal heart monitoring and an experienced operator in theatre
questions.exp: Ruptured membranes are the rule in established labour and are not a contraindication; the other conditions must all be met. (Book p552)

questions.sec: Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks
questions.q: Mechanism of breech delivery in RSA – engagement and descent:
opts: The buttocks engage in the right oblique diameter and the anterior buttock rotates forward under Hart's rule
The buttocks engage in the antero-posterior diameter and rotate through two-eighths of a circle
The sacrum engages transversely and rotates through three-eighths of a circle
The buttocks engage in the left oblique diameter and descend without any rotation
questions.exp: With the sacrum anterior the buttocks engage in the right oblique diameter and the anterior buttock descends and rotates forwards. (Book p553)

questions.sec: Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks
questions.q: In breech, which part lies directly behind the pubic symphysis, and what is unique about the denominator?
opts: The anterior buttock; breech is the exception where the denominator does not lie behind the symphysis
The sacrum itself, with the denominator behind the symphysis as it is in vertex
The posterior buttock, with the sacrum pointing anteriorly
The feet, which is why a breech has no denominator at all
questions.exp: In breech the anterior buttock lies behind the symphysis, and the sacrum as denominator is the exception to the general rule. (Book p553)

questions.sec: Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks
questions.q: When spontaneous delivery of the buttocks does not occur — match the manoeuvre to the breech type: complete breech : frank breech.
opts: Complete breech: groin traction — frank breech: Pinard's manoeuvre in the popliteal fossa
Complete breech: Pinard's manoeuvre — frank breech: groin traction
Complete breech: Lovset's manoeuvre — frank breech: Pinard's manoeuvre
Complete breech: Bracht's manoeuvre — frank breech: groin traction
questions.exp: A complete breech is delivered by traction in the groin; with extended legs the knees must be unlocked first by Pinard's manoeuvre. (Book p553)

questions.sec: Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks
questions.q: The Savage technique in breech delivery:
opts: Wrapping the baby's lower body in a warm moist towel so the cord is not handled and vasospasm is avoided
Suprapubic pressure applied to the fetal head to keep it flexed during delivery of the after-coming head
Fundal pressure applied by an assistant to push the shoulders down through the pelvic brim
Rotating the fetal trunk through 180 degrees to bring the shoulders into the oblique diameter
questions.exp: The Savage technique keeps the baby warm and prevents handling of the cord, since touching it provokes vasospasm and fetal distress. (Book p553)

questions.sec: Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks
questions.q: Fill up: With the sacrum anterior, the breech engages in the oblique diameter of the inlet with the ______ diameter leading.
opts: bitrochanteric
bisacromial
biparietal
submento-bregmatic
questions.exp: The bitrochanteric diameter (about 10 cm) is the engaging diameter of the breech, just as the bisacromial diameter serves the shoulders. (Book p553)

questions.sec: Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre
questions.q: Shoulder delivery in breech – the bisacromial diameter (12 cm) engages along the ______; the anterior shoulder touches levator ani and rotates ______.
opts: Right oblique diameter; anteriorly by 1/8th of a circle
Transverse diameter; posteriorly by 2/8th
AP diameter; not at all
Left oblique; 3/8th
questions.exp: Bisacromial 12 cm along right oblique; anterior shoulder rotates anteriorly 1/8th; anterior shoulder then posterior shoulder/arm deliver. (Book p554)

questions.sec: Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre
questions.q: If the shoulders are not along the AP diameter, the first step is:
opts: Hold the baby's back and rotate the shoulders into the antero-posterior diameter, then await spontaneous delivery
Perform Lovset's manoeuvre immediately without first rotating the shoulders
Apply fundal pressure to push the shoulders down through the pelvic brim
Apply Piper's forceps to deliver the head before the shoulders are released
questions.exp: If the shoulders are not in the antero-posterior diameter, rotate them there first; only if that fails move to Lovset's manoeuvre. (Book p554)

questions.sec: Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre
questions.q: Lovset's manoeuvre involves:
opts: Fingers over the baby's back rotate the trunk so the posterior shoulder comes forward and delivers
Traction on the groin to bring the breech down onto the pelvic floor
Pressure in the popliteal fossa to flex the knee and deliver the leg
Suprapubic pressure while the baby hangs by its own weight to deliver the head
questions.exp: Lovset's manoeuvre rotates the trunk through 180 degrees so that first the posterior and then the anterior shoulder is released. (Book p554)

questions.sec: Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre
questions.q: If Lovset's manoeuvre fails:
opts: Reach the cubital fossa with two fingers and deliver the arm
Apply Piper's forceps to the arm
Perform Zavanelli manoeuvre
Cleidotomy
questions.exp: Failure of Lovset's → reach cubital fossa with 2 fingers and sweep the arm down. (Book p554)

questions.sec: Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre
questions.q: Which of the following statements about delivering the shoulders in a breech birth is TRUE?
opts: Lovset's manoeuvre rotates the trunk so that the shoulders lie in the oblique diameter and the anterior shoulder is delivered first
Lovset's manoeuvre is used to flex and deliver the after-coming head
The bisacromial diameter normally engages in the antero-posterior diameter of the outlet
The arms should be pulled down as soon as the axilla becomes visible, without rotating the trunk
questions.exp: Lovset's manoeuvre turns the posterior shoulder to the front through 180 degrees so that the anterior shoulder slips under the symphysis. (Book p554)

questions.q: The after-coming head of breech is the ______ part delivered and is delivered by ______.
opts: Last; flexion
First; extension
Last; extension
Second; rotation
questions.exp: Head is the last part, delivered by flexion (opposite to vertex which delivers by extension). (Book p554)

questions.q: Burns-Marshall technique sequence:
opts: The baby hangs by its own weight, then suprapubic pressure with the feet swung towards the mother's abdomen delivers the head
Two fingers are placed in the baby's mouth and traction is applied to the shoulders to flex the head
Piper's forceps are applied to the after-coming head while the body rests along the operator's arm
The baby's back is held upwards and the trunk is rotated to bring the head into the transverse diameter
questions.exp: Burns-Marshall relies on controlled hanging with suprapubic pressure and swinging the body upwards to deliver the head by flexion. (Book p554)

questions.q: Bracht technique differs from Burns-Marshall in that:
opts: Suprapubic pressure is not given
Baby is not allowed to hang
Forceps are used
Malar flexion is added
questions.exp: Bracht = Burns-Marshall without suprapubic pressure. (Book p555)

questions.q: Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit technique combines:
opts: Traction on the shoulders with malar flexion, the baby astride the operator's forearm
Traction in the groin with flexion of the neck from above
Fundal pressure from an assistant combined with jaw traction
Rotation of the trunk with suprapubic pressure applied to the head
questions.exp: The Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit manoeuvre rests the baby on the forearm, flexes the head with fingers on the malar bones and applies shoulder traction. (Book p555)

questions.q: Piper's forceps are:
opts: Long forceps with pelvic, cephalic and perineal curves, used for the after-coming head
Short outlet forceps used for a head already on the pelvic floor
Rotational forceps with a sliding lock for a transverse head
Solid-blade forceps designed for a preterm after-coming head
questions.exp: Piper's forceps are long, with a perineal curve, and are applied to the after-coming head while an assistant holds the body up. (Book p555)

questions.q: Prague manoeuvre is used for delivery of the head in ______ position, where the head is delivered by ______; the m/c position is ______ (head by flexion).
opts: Dorso-posterior; extension; dorso-anterior
Dorso-anterior; flexion; dorso-posterior
LSA; flexion; RSA
Mento-posterior; flexion; mento-anterior
questions.exp: Dorso-posterior → Prague manoeuvre (head by extension); dorso-anterior m/c (head by flexion). Head occupies opposite oblique to shoulders/buttocks. (Book p555)

questions.q: Match the manoeuvre with how the after-coming head is delivered — 1) Burns-Marshall technique 2) Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit manoeuvre 3) Piper's forceps … A) Two fingers on the maxilla flex the head while an assistant holds the body up and applies suprapubic pressure B) The baby is allowed to hang by its own weight so that the head flexes and delivers spontaneously C) Forceps are applied to the after-coming head while an assistant holds the baby's body out of the way
questions.exp: Burns-Marshall uses controlled hanging, Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit uses jaw flexion and suprapubic pressure, and Piper's forceps rescue a trapped head. (Book p555)

questions.sec: Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction
questions.q: Entrapped after-coming head – preterm breech : term breech.
opts: Preterm: Duhrssen incisions in the cervix at 2 and 10 o'clock — term: push the body back and deliver by caesarean
Preterm: push the body back and deliver by caesarean — term: Duhrssen incisions in the cervix at 2 and 10 o'clock
Preterm: immediate craniotomy to allow vaginal delivery — term: Zavanelli manoeuvre then caesarean section
Both preterm and term: Piper's forceps are the first and only option for the trapped head
questions.exp: Before viability the cervix is incised to release the head; at term the body is pushed back and the baby is delivered by caesarean. (Book p555)

questions.sec: Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction
questions.q: Complications of breech delivery and the m/c cause of death:
opts: Intracranial haemorrhage is the commonest cause of death, with asphyxia and intra-abdominal injury
Shoulder dystocia is the commonest cause of death, with brachial plexus injury
Erb's palsy is the commonest cause of death, from traction on the extended arms
Fracture of the femur is the commonest cause of death in vaginal breech delivery
questions.exp: Rapid decompression and trapping of the after-coming head cause intracranial haemorrhage, the leading cause of death in breech. (Book p555)

questions.sec: Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction
questions.q: Breech extraction is indicated in:
opts: Twin pregnancy with the 1st twin cephalic and the 2nd in transverse lie
Singleton frank breech presenting at term in a primigravida
A footling breech in a primigravida at term, before labour
A preterm breech presenting before 34 completed weeks of gestation
questions.exp: Breech extraction is indicated in twin pregnancy with the first twin cephalic and the second twin in transverse lie. (Book p556)

questions.sec: Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction
questions.q: Method of breech extraction:
opts: Deliver the first twin vaginally, then internal podalic version followed by breech extraction under anaesthesia in theatre
External cephalic version of the second twin, then an oxytocin infusion to deliver vaginally
Immediate caesarean section for the second twin as soon as the first twin has been born
Wait for spontaneous delivery of the second twin without any intervention for up to two hours
questions.exp: Breech extraction is performed in theatre under anaesthesia, because all the manoeuvres are done by the operator with no maternal effort. (Book p556)

questions.sec: Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction
questions.q: All of the following are recognised fetal complications of vaginal breech delivery EXCEPT:
opts: Neonatal hypoglycaemia from maternal diabetes
Erb's palsy from traction on the extended arms
Intracranial haemorrhage from rapid decompression of the after-coming head
Fracture of the humerus, femur or clavicle during manipulation
questions.exp: Neonatal hypoglycaemia is a metabolic complication of diabetic pregnancy, not a mechanical complication of breech delivery. (Book p556)

questions.q: Indications for instrumental delivery (with station ≥ +2):
opts: Prolonged second stage, fetal distress, and shortening the second stage for maternal disease
A prolonged first stage, and cephalopelvic disproportion in established labour
Breech presentation, and a transverse lie with the arm prolapsed
Placenta previa, and cord prolapse with the cervix only 4 cm dilated
questions.exp: Instrumental delivery is for the second stage: delay, fetal distress, or a maternal indication to avoid pushing. (Book p557)

questions.q: Prerequisites mnemonic FORCEPS – expand it:
opts: Fully dilated os; Occiput/favourable position; Rotated head and Ruptured membranes; Consent and Contractions; Episiotomy, Engaged, Empty bladder; Pelvis adequate; CPD absent
Forceps blades ready; Obstetrician experienced; Room prepared; Consent obtained; Epidural sited; Pelvis assessed; Scissors available
Full term gestation; Occiput anterior; Rupture the membranes; Catheterise the bladder; Episiotomy cut; Push with pains; Stitch the perineum
Fetal heart checked; Oxygen running; Rotate the head fully; Cut an episiotomy; Extract the head; Pull steadily; Suture the tear afterwards
questions.exp: FORCEPS expands as: Fully dilated os; Occiput/favourable position; Rotated head + Ruptured membranes; Consent + Contracting uterus; Episiotomy + Engaged head + Empty bladder; Pelvis adequate; CPD absent. (Book p557)

questions.q: Favourable position for instrumental delivery:
opts: Sagittal suture anteroposterior, rotation up to 45°, station at least +2
Sagittal suture anteroposterior, rotation up to 45°, station above +2
Any occipito-transverse position, rotation up to 45°, station at +2
Sagittal suture transverse, rotation up to 45°, station at least +2
questions.exp: A favourable position for instrumental delivery is the sagittal suture in the anteroposterior diameter with rotation of at most 45° (DOA, DOP, ROA, LOA) and station +2 or more. (Book p557)

questions.q: Forceps vs vacuum – prerequisites differ how?
opts: Forceps require every prerequisite; vacuum may be used from 6 cm dilatation with an unrotated head
Vacuum requires every prerequisite; forceps may be used from 6 cm dilatation
Both instruments require full cervical dilatation before they can be applied
Forceps may be applied to an unengaged head, but the vacuum may never be
questions.exp: Vacuum extraction is more forgiving: it can be used before full dilatation and does not require the head to be rotated. (Book p557)

questions.q: Best-suited case for vacuum and the choice in maternal heart disease:
opts: A vertex with a fully dilated cervix and a rotated head; forceps are preferred in heart disease
A face presentation with the chin anterior; vacuum is preferred in heart disease
A breech presentation, where vacuum is preferred in maternal heart disease
A brow presentation, where forceps are preferred in maternal heart disease
questions.exp: Vacuum suits a rotated vertex at full dilatation; when maternal effort must be minimised, as in heart disease, forceps are preferred. (Book p557)

questions.q: Fill up: Prerequisites for instrumental delivery include full cervical dilatation, ruptured membranes, an empty bladder and a head at or below the level of the ______.
opts: ischial spines
pelvic inlet
sacral promontory
pelvic floor
questions.exp: The head must be at station zero or below, with the position known, the pelvis adequate and no disproportion before any instrument is applied. (Book p557)

questions.q: Contraindications specific to VACUUM:
opts: A preterm fetus, intrauterine death with a macerated head, the after-coming head and face presentation
Maternal heart disease, pregnancy-induced hypertension and a previous caesarean scar
An occipito-anterior position with the head already on the pelvic floor at full dilatation
A multiparous woman with a previously normal vaginal delivery at term
questions.exp: Vacuum-specific contraindications reflect scalp injury risk: prematurity, a macerated head, the after-coming head and malpresentation. (Book p558)

questions.q: Absolute contraindications to any instrumental delivery:
opts: Cephalopelvic disproportion, an unengaged head, and a fetus with a bleeding disorder or bone demineralisation
Prolonged second stage, maternal exhaustion and an epidural already sited for pain relief
Maternal cardiac disease, pregnancy-induced hypertension and one previous caesarean section
Occipito-posterior position, a loose nuchal cord and lightly stained meconium liquor
questions.exp: Absolute contraindications reflect disproportion, an unengaged head and fetal fragility; exhaustion and a long second stage are indications, not contraindications. (Book p558)

questions.q: Silastic cups – advantages and pressures:
opts: Safer and easier to apply; pressure starts at 0.2 kg/cm2 and is raised to 0.8 kg/cm2 over about two minutes
Metal cups that are more traumatic, built up to 1.5 kg/cm2 over ten minutes
Rigid cups applied to a pressure of 0.5 kg/cm2 reached instantly
Disposable cups with the maximum pressure limited to 0.1 kg/cm2
questions.exp: Silastic cups cause less scalp trauma and are applied with negative pressure rising gradually to 0.8 kg/cm2 (600 mmHg). (Book p558)

questions.q: Correct application of the vacuum cup:
opts: Centre the cup over the flexion point, about 6 cm behind the anterior fontanelle and 3 cm in front of the posterior one
Centre the cup over the anterior fontanelle, so the head deflexes as traction is applied to the skull
Centre the cup over the posterior fontanelle, which is the flexion point for vacuum application
Centre the cup over the parietal eminence on whichever side of the head lies against the sacrum
questions.exp: Correct placement is over the flexion point on the sagittal suture, which promotes flexion and minimises scalp trauma and cup detachment. (Book p558)

questions.q: All of the following are contraindications to vacuum extraction EXCEPT:
opts: A cephalic presentation at full dilatation with the head engaged in the occipito-anterior position
Gestational age below 34 weeks, because of the risk of scalp and intracranial injury
A known fetal bleeding disorder or bone demineralisation
A face or brow presentation with an ill-defined flexion point
questions.exp: An engaged cephalic presentation at full dilatation is the indication for vacuum extraction; prematurity, coagulopathy and malpresentation are not. (Book p558)

questions.q: The Omnicup is:
opts: A newer, smaller, portable disposable vacuum device used for occipito-anterior and posterior positions
A metal cup designed for delivery of the face presentation
A rotational forceps with a sliding lock for the transverse head
A fetal scalp electrode used to monitor the heart rate in labour
questions.exp: The Omnicup is a modern handheld vacuum device suitable for both occipito-anterior and occipito-posterior positions. (Book p559)

questions.q: Parts of obstetric forceps include:
opts: Handle, finger guard, lock, shank, heel and a fenestrated blade with pelvic and cephalic curves
Cup, chain, handle and hand pump for generating negative pressure
Blade, ratchet, teeth and serrations for gripping the fetal head firmly
Handle, spring and hook for applying traction to the fetal scalp
questions.exp: Each blade has a handle with finger guard, a lock, a shank, a heel and a fenestrated blade with pelvic and cephalic curves. (Book p559)

questions.q: Advantages of fenestrations (windows) in the blade:
opts: Lighter blades that grip well while compressing the fetal head less
Stronger traction through a wider surface of metal on the head
Rotation of the head by allowing the blades to slide independently
A better grip on the fetal scalp to prevent the blades slipping
questions.exp: Fenestration lightens the blade and reduces the compressive force transmitted to the fetal head without losing grip. (Book p559)

questions.q: Types of lock — English lock (most common) : sliding lock.
opts: English: two sockets, with the left blade introduced first — sliding: one socket that lets the blades slide
English: a single socket — sliding: two sockets with the right blade introduced first
English: a screw mechanism — sliding: a pivot joint between the two shanks
English: no lock at all — sliding: a ratchet that locks at fixed intervals
questions.exp: The English lock has a socket on each handle and closes only when the left blade goes in first; the sliding lock corrects asynclitism. (Book p559)

questions.q: Left/right forceps identification:
opts: Named for the mother's left and right; held correctly the left socket faces up and the right socket faces down
Named for the operator's hands, with both sockets facing upwards when applied
Identified by blade length, since the left blade is noticeably longer
Identified by colour coding on the handle of each blade
questions.exp: Forceps blades are named for the side of the mother's pelvis; held correctly, the left blade's socket faces upwards. (Book p560)

questions.q: Correctly applied forceps are identified by:
opts: The lock closes easily and both blades lie equidistant from the sagittal suture along the occipito-mental diameter
The blades overlap slightly in the midline over the region of the anterior fontanelle
One blade lies over the face and the other over the occiput to grip the head firmly
The handles sit at 90 degrees to each other because the head is lying transversely
questions.exp: Correct application means the lock closes without force, the blades sit symmetrically along the occipito-mental diameter and the sagittal suture is midway. (Book p560)

questions.q: Wrigley forceps:
opts: Outlet forceps; short and light; total length 27.5 cm, shank 2.5 cm
Long rotational forceps; total length 35 cm, sliding lock
Forceps for the aftercoming head; total length 27.5 cm
Solid-bladed forceps; short and light, shank 2.5 cm
questions.exp: Wrigley forceps are outlet forceps, short and light, with a total length of 27.5 cm and a shank of 2.5 cm. (Book p560)

questions.q: Kielland forceps:
opts: Long, the only forceps that can rotate the head, with a sliding lock; outdated
Short outlet forceps with a fixed English lock and no rotation; still used
Longest forceps designed for the aftercoming head in breech; still used
Solid-bladed forceps with a fixed English lock and no rotation; outdated
questions.exp: Kielland forceps are long, are the only forceps that can rotate the fetal head (rotation forceps), have a sliding lock, and are now largely outdated. (Book p560)

questions.q: Match — Piper's forceps : Tucker-McLane forceps.
opts: Piper's: the longest forceps, for the after-coming head — Tucker-McLane: the only forceps with a solid blade
Piper's: a solid blade for the head — Tucker-McLane: for the after-coming head
Piper's: a short outlet forceps — Tucker-McLane: the rotational forceps
Piper's: a sliding lock — Tucker-McLane: the shortest forceps available
questions.exp: Piper's are long forceps with a perineal curve for the after-coming head; Tucker-McLane are the only forceps with solid blades. (Book p560)

questions.q: Match the forceps with its distinguishing feature — 1) Kielland's forceps 2) Piper's forceps 3) Simpson's forceps … A) A sliding lock with almost no pelvic curve, designed for rotation of the head B) Long forceps with a perineal curve for the after-coming head in a breech delivery C) Standard outlet forceps with both a pelvic and a cephalic curve for the flexed head
questions.exp: Kielland's slides to correct asynclitism and rotates, Piper's reaches the after-coming head, and Simpson's follows the curves of the pelvis and head. (Book p560)

questions.sec: Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
questions.q: Low forceps (m/c type) vs outlet (Wrigley) forceps criteria:
opts: Low forceps: station +2 or more without reaching the perineum — outlet forceps: scalp visible at the introitus with the skull on the pelvic floor
Low forceps: at the level of the ischial spines — outlet forceps: station +1 with the head still above the pelvic floor
Low forceps: crowning with the head distending the perineum — outlet forceps: station +2 or lower inside the cavity
Low forceps: any station with the head not yet engaged — outlet forceps: the head still above the level of the ischial spines
questions.exp: Low forceps are the commonest type and are applied at station +2 or more; outlet forceps are only used when the scalp is visible. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
questions.q: Mid-cavity forceps (0/+1 station) and high forceps (−ve station) are:
opts: Obsolete
Standard practice
Used only in twins
Used with Kielland only
questions.exp: Mid-cavity and high forceps are obsolete. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
questions.q: Direction of pull – ideal position and basis; low forceps pulls : outlet forceps pulls.
opts: Low forceps: downward and backward, then downward, then downward and forward
Outlet forceps in lithotomy: downward, then downward and forward
Low forceps in the supine position: upward, then forward throughout
Outlet forceps in left lateral position: forward only throughout the pull
questions.exp: Pull is directed in lithotomy with the operator's hand on the maternal abdomen; low forceps pull downward and backward, then downward, then downward and forward, while outlet forceps pull downward then downward and forward. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
questions.q: Prior to forceps delivery:
opts: Consent, adequate analgesia by epidural or pudendal block, and episiotomy
General anaesthesia, which is mandatory for all forceps deliveries
An oxytocin bolus given immediately before the blades are applied
A urinary catheter left in situ throughout the whole procedure
questions.exp: Prior to forceps delivery one must obtain consent, give adequate analgesia (epidural or pudendal block) and perform an episiotomy. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
questions.q: Fill up: Low forceps are applied when the leading point of the fetal skull is at station ______ or lower, while outlet forceps are applied when the scalp is visible at the introitus.
questions.exp: Low forceps means station +2 or more; outlet forceps are applied only when the scalp is visible without separating the labia. (Book p561)

questions.sec: Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
questions.q: Traction force for forceps – primigravida : multigravida.
opts: 8 kg : 5 kg
questions.exp: Primi 16–18 kg; multi 12–13 kg. (Book p562)

questions.sec: Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
questions.q: M/c complication – forceps : vacuum; ease of use:
opts: Maternal injury : fetal injury; forceps require more training, vacuum easier (m/c used)
Fetal injury : maternal injury; vacuum harder
Both maternal; equal
Both fetal; forceps easier
questions.exp: Forceps → maternal injury; vacuum → fetal injury; vacuum easier and m/c used. (Book p562)

questions.sec: Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
questions.q: Fetal complications – forceps : vacuum.
opts: Forceps: facial nerve palsy and corneal injury — vacuum: cephalhaematoma and subgaleal haemorrhage
Forceps: sixth nerve palsy and subgaleal bleed — vacuum: facial nerve palsy and corneal injury
Forceps: cephalhaematoma only — vacuum: corneal abrasion only
Forceps: subgaleal haemorrhage — vacuum: brachial plexus injury from the shoulders
questions.exp: Forceps injure the face and skull base; the vacuum produces scalp injuries, notably cephalhaematoma and subgaleal haemorrhage. (Book p562)

questions.sec: Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
questions.q: Failed forceps/vacuum is defined as ______ and managed by ______.
opts: 3 unsuccessful trials to deliver the head; C-section
1 failed pull; switch instrument
5 failed pulls; symphysiotomy
10 min without delivery; oxytocin
questions.exp: 3 unsuccessful attempts = failed instrumental delivery → C-section. (Book p562)

units.title: Breech: features, incidence, causes & types
units.guide: Track breech incidence by gestation, its m/c causes, and distinguish complete, frank, knee and footling breech by posture, P/V findings and cord-prolapse risk. Focus for this checkpoint: Breech: features, incidence, causes & types.

units.title: Management of breech: USG, ECV & mode of delivery
units.guide: Use USG to screen for ECV, follow the ECV flowchart, and apply the absolute and relative indications for caesarean section. Focus for this checkpoint: Management of breech: USG, ECV & mode of delivery.

units.title: Assisted breech delivery: features, complication, C/I & prerequisites
units.guide: Know the denominator, engaging diameter and m/c position of breech, the deadly complication of the after-coming head, and the safety prerequisites. Focus for this checkpoint: Assisted breech delivery: features, complication, C/I & prerequisites.

units.title: Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks
units.guide: Follow the RSA mechanism from oblique engagement to spontaneous buttock delivery, and apply groin traction, Pinard's manoeuvre and the Savage technique. Focus for this checkpoint: Mechanism of breech delivery & manoeuvres for buttocks.

units.title: Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre
units.guide: Trace the bisacromial diameter through the pelvis and rescue extended arms with Lovset's manoeuvre or cubital fossa delivery. Focus for this checkpoint: Shoulder delivery in breech & Lovset's manoeuvre.

units.title: After-coming head of breech: manoeuvres
units.guide: Deliver the after-coming head with Burns-Marshall, Bracht, Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit, Piper's forceps and Prague manoeuvre – and know when each applies. Focus for this checkpoint: After-coming head of breech: manoeuvres.

units.title: Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction
units.guide: Manage the entrapped head differently in preterm and term breech, recall the m/c cause of death, and define breech extraction for the second twin. Focus for this checkpoint: Complications of breech delivery & breech extraction.

units.title: Instrumental delivery: indications, prerequisites & choice
units.guide: Learn the indications, the FORCEPS mnemonic of prerequisites, the favourable positions, and when vacuum can replace forceps. Focus for this checkpoint: Instrumental delivery: indications, prerequisites & choice.

units.title: Contraindications & vacuum delivery technique
units.guide: Recall the vacuum-specific and absolute contraindications, then set up the silastic cup pressures and the flexion-point application. Focus for this checkpoint: Contraindications & vacuum delivery technique.

units.title: Forceps: parts, locks, handedness & types
units.guide: Name the parts of the obstetric forceps, the two lock types, how to identify left from right, and the four classic forceps with their unique features. Focus for this checkpoint: Forceps: parts, locks, handedness & types.

units.title: Forceps application, direction of pull & complications
units.guide: Classify low vs outlet forceps, pull in the correct sequence of directions, quote traction forces, and compare complications of forceps and vacuum. Focus for this checkpoint: Forceps application, direction of pull & complications.
